Spanish Automotive Sector Records Steady Trade Figures in First Quarter

The Spanish automotive industry has reported stable trade figures for the first quarter of the year, according to data released this week by the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers (ANFAC). Despite a challenging global economic backdrop, Spain’s vehicle exports and imports have maintained their momentum, reinforcing the sector’s role as a key pillar of the national economy.

Between January and March, Spain exported 675,000 passenger and commercial vehicles, a slight increase of 1.8% compared to the same period last year. The total export value reached €10.2 billion, with France, Germany, and Italy remaining the three largest destinations for Spanish-made vehicles. Meanwhile, imports stood at 212,000 vehicles, up 2.1% year-on-year, reflecting resilient domestic demand.

María López, ANFAC’s director of economic affairs, attributed the steady figures to balanced supply chains and consistent demand across major European markets. “Our manufacturers have continued to adapt to evolving market needs, particularly in the electric and hybrid segments,” López said. “It’s encouraging to see stable exports, which help secure jobs and investment across Spain’s industrial regions.”

Electric and hybrid vehicles accounted for 14% of all exports, up from 11% in the first quarter of last year. According to Javier Gómez, an analyst at Iberia Vehicle Insights, this signals the industry’s ongoing transformation. “We’re seeing gradual but sustained growth in low-emission vehicle shipments, especially to Northern Europe,” Gómez noted.

Employment in Spain’s automotive manufacturing sector remained steady, with approximately 210,000 workers directly employed. Unions welcomed the latest data, emphasizing the importance of ongoing training and modernization. “The stability in trade figures is good news for our members,” said Juana Torres, spokesperson for the Federation of Automotive Workers. “We need to keep investing in skills to ensure our workforce stays at the forefront of technological change.”

The port of Barcelona, one of the country’s main export hubs, handled 23% of Spain’s outbound vehicle shipments, while other key ports included Valencia and Santander. Local officials highlighted the broader economic benefits. “The automotive sector supports thousands of jobs throughout the supply chain, from logistics to components manufacturing,” said Catalonia’s regional industry minister, Josep Ferrer.

Industry leaders remain cautiously optimistic for the remainder of the year, citing stable order books and robust demand in core markets. “We expect moderate growth to continue, provided current trends hold,” López added.
